comment: AI/ML lifecycle governance should be explicit across the architecture. Chapter 5 appropriately requires representative data, evaluation, human oversight and monitoring for model drift. Appendix C also provides strong lifecycle governance for computable decision logic. However, the architecture does not explicitly define how learned AI/ML models deployed through decision support, surveillance, analytics or point-of-service applications should be identified, versioned and linked to validation and monitoring evidence.

public.text: AI/ML lifecycle governance should be explicit across the architecture. Chapter 5 appropriately requires representative data, evaluation, human oversight and monitoring for model drift. Appendix C also provides strong lifecycle governance for computable decision logic. However, the architecture does not explicitly define how learned AI/ML models deployed through decision support, surveillance, analytics or point-of-service applications should be identified, versioned and linked to validation and monitoring evidence.
public.suggestedRevision: Define a cross-cutting AI/ML lifecycle governance profile rather than a mandatory central AI component. Consequential AI outputs should be traceable to a unique model identifier/version, accountable owner, intended use, validation population and context, relevant performance evidence, deployment status, human-oversight requirements, monitoring/drift criteria, and suspension/rollback/decommission status. Existing CDSE versioning, audit and rollback patterns can be referenced as an architectural precedent.
